paras: The lynching at Eros, Louisiana, was the reported killing in August 1905 of an unnamed Black man accused of being one of two men who shot and wounded J. H. Sanders, a merchant who was serving as a quarantine guard at Eros. According to a Monroe dispatch, he was lynched on the night of August 11, and the second accused man was to be lynched as soon as he was caught. The story reached readers only as a brief wire item in white newspapers from Washington to Michigan, and no follow-up was found.

Sanders, whose name some papers spelled "Saunders," was described as a merchant at Eros who was acting as a quarantine guard when he was shot. The reports do not say why he was shot, who fired, or what race he was, beyond calling his assailants "negroes."

On August 12 a correspondent at Monroe, Louisiana, sent word of "reports received here to-day from Eros" that one of the men who had shot Sanders had been lynched. The version carried as the New Orleans Picayune's special placed the lynching "last night," that is, August 11, and called Sanders "dangerously wounded." A shorter version printed in Washington, New York and Richmond gave no date and called him "seriously wounded."

None of the reports names the man who was killed or says how he was caught, who killed him, how many took part, or how he died. The Picayune version added that "the other negro, it is said, will be lynched as soon as captured."
No report of an inquest, arrests, the capture of the second man, or Sanders's recovery appears in the coverage.

White papers printed the item on August 13 under headlines that put race first, among them "One Negro Lynched, Another Likely to Be" in the Louisville Courier-Journal, "Another Negro Lynched" in the Montgomery Advertiser, and "Negro Shooter Lynched" in the New-York Tribune. The Courier-Journal's subhead called the accused men "Miscreants," while the Washington Evening Star ran the story on its front page as "Lynching in Louisiana." Every version treated the shooting as established fact, referring to "the negroes who shot" Sanders, and none questioned the killing.

Within days the story shrank to a single paragraph in syndicated news-brief columns, appearing in the Ceredo Advance of West Virginia on August 16 and the Berea Citizen of Kentucky on August 17. By August 26 the Diamond Drill of Crystal Falls, Michigan, ran it as "Lynched for Shooting Guard," with a closing line saying the guard had been "killed." No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

The accounts differ on small points: the wounded man's name appears as both Sanders and Saunders, his wound as "dangerously" or "seriously" inflicted, and only the Picayune version dates the lynching. The Diamond Drill's statement that the guard was "killed" contradicts its own earlier wording and every other report, all of which describe him as wounded.

reader.title: Lynching at Eros, Louisiana (1905)
bases: Every report says one of the Black men accused of shooting J. H. Sanders 'was lynched', and the fullest version adds that a second man would be lynched when captured (A1, A2, A3).

The reports say a Black man accused of shooting a merchant acting as quarantine guard was 'lynched' in reprisal, which implies an extralegal killing for an alleged crime (A1, A2, A3); but they rest on second-hand 'reports received' at Monroe and give no account of the killers, their number or the method (A1, A6).

All nine items trace to Monroe, La., dispatches of Aug. 12 relaying unconfirmed 'reports' from Eros, in two textual forms (the Picayune special, A1, A3, and a shorter version, A2, A4, A6); no local, independent or follow-up report was found.

accounts.label: Picayune's Monroe special
accounts.gist: Reports from Eros said one of the negroes who shot and dangerously wounded Sanders was lynched the night of Aug. 11, and that the other would be lynched as soon as captured.

accounts.label: Short Monroe dispatch
accounts.gist: Reports from Eros said one of the negroes who shot and seriously wounded Saunders had been lynched; no date for the lynching and no mention of the second man.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Monroe dispatch without comment under headlines such as 'One Negro Lynched, Another Likely to Be' and 'Another Negro Lynched', presenting the accusation against the dead man as settled ('the negroes who shot').
The New-York Tribune headlined it 'Negro Shooter Lynched' and the Richmond Times-Dispatch 'Negro Lynched', each with a subhead on the wounded quarantine guard.

conflicts.note: Spelling differs by dispatch version; no local report settles it.
The Diamond Drill's 'killed' contradicts its own 'seriously wounded' earlier in the same item and appears to be a rewriting error; all other versions say wounded.
Only the Picayune version dates it.
